raw_claim_fact: For aluminum brackets, China CNC machining typically costs US$15-55/part vs US$60-150/part in the US; China prototype (1-50pcs) lead time ~3-7 working days, low-volume (50-200pcs) ~7-10 days plus 3-5 days air freight; US suppliers typically deliver in 5-14 business days. Cumulative China savings at scale often 30-50%, but 'at low quantities, US quoting efficiency and shorter setup overhead often match or beat the offshore unit price plus freight and compliance burden.'

One CNC-cost-comparison source explicitly cautions: 'Many China shops accept prototype and low-volume runs, so the real difference is usually smaller than buyers expect' — i.e. the China cost advantage narrows (not disappears) at true one-off/prototype scale.

China PCB fabrication for basic prototype orders runs ~US$10-50; for a 20-board run (5x3in, 30 BOM items, 60 SMT + 25 THT parts) per-board cost cited as ~$10 fab + $35 assembly; China PCB assembly offers a claimed 30-50% lower base cost, and even with 25-35% Section-301 tariffs (2025) still saves 15-25% for orders over 100 units.

'For small-batch prototyping (1-100 units), US local sourcing eliminates international shipping delays and extra tariff costs, making overall pricing more competitive for low-volume orders'; the volume crossover to China favor is cited at roughly 100-500+ units.

manufacturing_process: Injection molding; sheet metal (laser/bend/weld); die casting
raw_claim_fact: Multiple China-based manufacturing marketplaces/vendors (Xometry China ops, PCBWay, Qmolding, RpProto, Wayzao, UIDEA, Sung Precision Mould & Plastic) offer integrated prototype-through-low-volume services spanning CNC, injection molding, die casting, sheet-metal fabrication and 3D printing under one sourcing relationship, typically with flexible MOQs and online quoting.

US motor-manufacturing equipment (coil winders, taping machines, commutator undercutters, banding machines, TIG welders) is described as 'now decades old and operating well past the point where reactive maintenance can keep up' amid a reshoring wave of ~US$1.662 trillion in announced manufacturing commitments (131 companies, 32 states) since Jan 2025.

The 'Pedro' open-source project is a fully open-source 3D-printable educational robot arm with 6 rotational joints and a parallel-jaw gripper, using 7x Feetech STS3215 serial-bus servos, with a stated build cost of approximately US$220.

A US manufacturing-marketplace guide advises that robot-arm 'primary structural link bodies and actuator housings use CNC for prototype through pilot; bearing seats and precision mating interfaces use CNC; and secondary brackets use sheet metal' — explicit process-selection guidance aimed at exactly the maker/small-integrator audience named in the issue.

The issue instructs not to assume a 3D-printing-driven trend without evidence. This research pass found direct evidence that at least some notable open-source maker robot-arm projects (Pedro, reBot-DevArm, and others catalogued at orobot.io) do center on FDM 3D printing for structural parts, but found no quantitative source (e.g. survey of maker robot builds by fabrication method) establishing what share of maker/startup robot builds use 3D printing vs CNC vs off-the-shelf extrusion.
